steps.name: First appointment
steps.text: Cloth, style and measurements. About an hour.
steps.more: We look at how you stand and how you'll wear it, choose the cloth together and take some thirty measurements. Bring a jacket you like and the shoes you'll wear with the suit.

steps.name: Cut
steps.text: Your pattern drafted by hand, then the cloth cut.
steps.more: Your cutter drafts a paper pattern from the measurements and cuts the cloth from it. The pattern is kept in your name for every commission after this one.

photo.alt: A cutter drawing on a paper pattern on the cutting table

steps.name: Baste fitting
steps.text: The coat held in white thread, to be taken apart.
steps.more: About four weeks after the first appointment. The coat is loosely sewn so the cutter can mark changes in chalk, unpick it and recut where needed.

photo.alt: A coat in progress on a tailor's stand in the workroom, the tailor at his bench behind

steps.name: Forward fitting
steps.text: Lining and pockets in; the last changes.
steps.more: Four to six weeks later. The coat is nearly finished; sleeves, collar and length are settled and the buttons chosen.

photo.alt: Four horn buttons in an open hand

steps.name: Finished
steps.more: A last try-on, a final press, and the coat is yours. Most first commissions take ten to twelve weeks; later ones are quicker.

photo.alt: A finished camel jacket on a hanger by a window

explained.title: Bespoke or made to measure
explained.intro: Both are made to order. What differs is the pattern, the fittings and the hand work.

rows.label: The pattern
rows.bespoke: Drafted for you alone by your cutter.
rows.mtm: A standard pattern, altered to your measurements.

rows.label: Fittings
rows.bespoke: A series of fittings. Here, usually three.

sections.heading: Why the word isn't enough
sections.body: In 2008 the UK's Advertising Standards Authority found that "bespoke" could be used for made-to-measure suits, since both are made to order. So the word alone doesn't tell you how a suit is made: ask who drafts the pattern and how many fittings you'll have.

sections.heading: Which is right for you
sections.body: Made to measure can be quicker and costs less. Bespoke suits a figure or a wish a standard pattern can't meet, and gets better with each commission because the pattern is kept and refined.

items.title: Choosing cloth by season
items.author: Edmund, head cutter
items.summary: Heavier for winter, open weaves for summer, and one cloth that works all year.

photo.alt: Rust hopsack folded over a sand cloth

items.body:
Weight is the first thing to look at. Heavier cloths, like a tweed or a milled flannel, are warm and drape well; they suit coats and winter suits.

For summer, look for open weaves that let air through: hopsack and linen. Linen creases, and that is part of it.

If you will own one suit, a mid-weight worsted in navy or grey works through most of the year. Bring the swatches home before you decide; cloth looks different in daylight.

items.title: What to wear to a wedding
items.author: Rosa, cutter
items.summary: Start with the invitation, then leave time for three fittings.

photo.alt: Four horn buttons in an open hand

items.body:
Read the invitation first. Morning dress, black tie and lounge suits are all asked for by name; if it says nothing, a well-cut lounge suit is right.

If you are in the wedding party, agree the cloth together early: a whole party in one cloth means one order with the mill and fittings planned around the day.

Count back from the date. A first commission needs about three fittings, and a party needs more time to measure and cut everyone. The wedding planner on this site does the counting.

items.title: Looking after a suit
items.author: Tomasz, coatmaker
items.summary: Rest it, brush it, hang it well, and clean it rarely.

photo.alt: Jackets in tweed and check on copper hangers

items.body:
Give a suit a day off between wears so the cloth can recover its shape.

Hang the coat on a shaped hanger that fills the shoulders, and brush it after wearing to lift dust from the weave.

Clean it only when it needs it; pressing between cleans keeps it sharp. If the coat needs letting out, bring it to us: there is extra cloth in the seams for that.
